initial_presentation: A 55-year-old woman was referred to the neurologist due to worsening cognitive issues, including forgetfulness and reduced concentration over the past year. In the week leading up to her admission, she experienced significant headaches along with auditory and visual hallucinations. Upon admission, she exhibited aphasia, particularly with word-finding difficulties. She was disoriented and demonstrated impaired memory and visuospatial abilities. There were no signs of pyramidal or extrapyramidal involvement, myoclonic jerks, or cerebellar symptoms.

A 9-year-old girl presented to the Emergency Department 4 days after experiencing blunt trauma to her left leg. Upon admission, she was afebrile. Physical examination revealed an area of edema, warmth, erythema, and tenderness with indistinct margins on the anteromedial aspect of the left leg. The remainder of the physical examination was normal, except for obesity, and her medical history was unremarkable.

A 32-year-old woman presented with a painful swelling in the maxillary gingiva. She had a history of an inflammatory lesion at the same site and had used antibiotics 10 months prior. The lesion did not reduce in size. Following the extraction of the upper left second premolar, the lesion continued to grow. She was referred to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon. Extraoral examination showed facial asymmetry and the disappearance of the left nasolabial fold. Intraoral examination revealed a firm, sessile, pink exophytic ulcerative mass with a lobulated surface on the maxillary left buccal gingiva, extending from the canine to the distal of the first molar. The lesion was tender and bled easily upon palpation. The first premolar was mobile.

A five-year-old female with brown skin has had erythematous-hyperchromic plaques with slightly raised edges and an atrophic center on the face (bilateral malar areas, lower eyelids, nose, and chin) since she was one and a half years old. Similar lesions with more pronounced borders are present on the dorsal area of the left hand and the lateral side of the second digit of the right hand. Dermatologic examination revealed that the lower eyelid lesions extended to the eye mucosa, initiating ectropion growth. The left nasal lesion had a meliceric crust due to a recent impetigo process, which is currently being treated. There are no significant personal medical history details. Examination of family members showed no notable skin changes.

A 51-year-old man with a 20-year history of consuming 1.5 liters of beer daily, often accompanied by 360 mL of shochu, and a 4-year history of reduced appetite, developed slurred speech over a 3-week period. He experienced choking while drinking and difficulty swallowing food, eventually becoming unable to eat or drink, leading to his admission. His medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and previous burr-hole drainage for bilateral chronic subdural hematomas at age 44, after which he was independent in daily activities. On admission, his blood pressure was 112/79 mmHg, height was 183 cm, and weight was 48 kg. Neurological examination showed he was alert with a mini-mental status examination (MMSE) score of 22 points. He had horizontal gaze paretic nystagmus bilaterally, a flat facial expression, and bilateral weakness of the orbicularis oris. There was no weakness in the frontalis muscle or orbicularis oculi. His speech was slurred, and he had difficulty swallowing, with poor gag reflex and palate elevation. The jaw jerk reflex was brisk, and the snout reflex was positive. There was no emotional lability, tongue atrophy, or fasciculation. The tongue could protrude midline and move adequately side to side. Motor weakness was noted with scores of 4 in the distal upper limbs and 3 in the proximal lower limbs bilaterally on the Modified Medical Research Council’s manual muscle test (MMT). Bilateral finger-to-nose incoordination was present. He could not walk due to a wide-based gait with truncal instability. Deep tendon reflexes in the upper limbs were increased, and Babinski reflexes were positive bilaterally. Hoffmann reflexes and the forced grasp reflex were negative. Superficial vibratory and position senses were normal.

An 18-month-old Caucasian boy was referred with a history of spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeds starting at nine months old. Initial complete blood count revealed a low platelet count, and he was previously diagnosed with ITP. There were no abnormalities in child development or physical examination, and there was no family history of bleeding. He was the only child of nonconsanguineous parents.

A 36-year-old woman underwent a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) in 2017 and a laparoscopic revision to a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) in August 2019 due to persistent gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) with reflux esophagitis. Her surgical history also includes a laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 2018. She was prescribed a multivitamin supplement and was not on any other medication. Six weeks post-surgery, she experienced severe colicky pain in the right upper abdomen multiple times. Her food intake was moderate, affected by nausea, vomiting, flatulence, and regurgitation of food despite using a proton pump inhibitor. Physical examination revealed normal hemodynamic values: heart rate of 75 beats per minute, temperature of 36.9ºC, blood pressure of 135/74 mmHg, oxygen saturation of 98%, and respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute. Pressure pain was noted in the right upper abdomen.

A 7-year-old Polynesian female child presented with a swelling in the left preauricular area that had grown over a period of 3 months. Physical examination revealed a 2 cm × 2 cm firm, elevated, non-painful mass that moved in conjunction with the mandible. No occlusal alterations or additional significant clinical findings were noted.

A 23-year-old female presented with a 6-month history of chest pain, dry cough, hoarseness of voice, and recent onset of stridor. The chest pain was retrosternal, severe, continuous, radiated to the back, and was associated with shortness of breath on mild exertion. The cough was dry, intermittent, and progressively worsened over time, accompanied by hoarseness of voice, recent stridor, and dysphagia mainly for fluids. There was no history of fever, hemoptysis, night sweating, or weight loss. The patient had no history of smoking, recent travel, or contact with tuberculosis patients. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities.

A 33-year-old male presented with reduced vision in his right eye for a duration of 6 days. He was referred from another center with concerns about serous retinal detachment. His medical history includes a diagnosis of MS 7 years prior, for which he received intramuscular interferon beta 1a therapy [Avonex®, 30 µg (6 million IU) once a week] for 2 years, but the treatment was discontinued due to side effects, and he has since been monitored without medication. His best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was recorded as 0.1 in the right eye and 1.0 in the left eye using a Snellen chart.
